Nanoplastics [5540]

By: Carol Albertyn Christie | Production

Proposal


Show:

Further information:
Plastic pollution is now so widespread that you may be ingesting 5g a week, the equivalent of eating a credit card, according to a study commissioned by the environmental charity WWF International.

The study by Australia's University of Newcastle said the largest source of plastic ingestion was from tap and especially bottled water.

In the United States, 94.4% of tap water samples contained plastic fibres, with an average of 9.6 fibres per litre.

European water was less polluted, with fibres showing up in only 72.2% of water samples, and only 3.8 fibres per litre.
Another major source was shellfish, which tended to be eaten whole so the plastic in their digestive system was consumed too. Nearly invisible bits of polymer were also found in beer and salt.

"Since 2000, the world has produced as much plastic as all the preceding years combined, a third of which is leaked into nature," the report said.

The average person could be consuming 1,769 particles of plastic every week from water alone, it said.

The findings, drawn from 52 peer-reviewed studies, are the first to estimate the sheer weight of plastics consumed by individual humans: about 250g over the course of a year.

The amount of plastic pollution varies by location, but nowhere is untouched, said the report.

Not only are plastics polluting our oceans and waterways and killing marine life, it's in all of us.

A study released last year by the Water Research Commission (WRC), done by North-West University researchers, found that our fresh water contains microplastics. The Crocodile River, which feeds the Hartbeespoort Dam before the water flows into the Limpopo, had the highest total particle, fragment and fibre counts, although the Vaal Dam water contained larger particles.

The study was done on rivers in North West, Gauteng and the Free State, and included drinking and groundwater sources.

Tap water in Johannesburg and Tshwane was found to contain the particles.

“Generally, much lower [levels of] particles were observed in treated water compared to the raw water. Tap water samples collected from the Tshwane region seemed to have fewer fragments compared with Johannesburg,” according to the study.

Following the release of the report, the department of environmental affairs said it would set up a task team of officials from the departments of trade and industry, health, and science and technology to find ways to reduce the use of these particulates.
All over the world, researchers like Magadini are staring through microscopes at tiny pieces of plastic—fibers, fragments, or microbeads—that have made their way into marine and freshwater species, both wild caught and farmed. Scientists have found microplastics in 114 aquatic species, and more than half of those end up on our dinner plates. Now they are trying to determine what that means for human health.

So far science lacks evidence that microplastics—pieces smaller than one-fifth of an inch—are affecting fish at the population level. Our food supply doesn’t seem to be under threat—at least as far as we know. But enough research has been done now to show that the fish and shellfish we enjoy are suffering from the omnipresence of this plastic. Every year five million to 14 million tons flow into our oceans from coastal areas. Sunlight, wind, waves, and heat break down that material into smaller bits that look—to plankton, bivalves, fish, and even whales—a lot like food.

Experiments show that microplastics damage aquatic creatures, as well as turtles and birds: They block digestive tracts, diminish the urge to eat, and alter feeding behavior, all of which reduce growth and reproductive output. Their stomachs stuffed with plastic, some species starve and die.

In addition to mechanical effects, microplastics have chemical impacts, because free-floating pollutants that wash off the land and into our seas—such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and heavy metals—tend to adhere to their surfaces.

Nanoplastics Script No 12 (To match Edit 12)

V/O
When you next raise a glass with your friends, there may be more in your beer than the buzz it gives.

Plastic has been with us for only about 70 years, yet it has become of the biggest man made disasters. When one thinks of plastic pollution, one often thinks about images like these. A hightide mark covered in plastic bottles.
But there are smaller pieces of plastic called microplastics, and 1000 times smaller than that there are microscopic nanoplastics, which we unavoidably eat and breath in.

Matt Coote is a marine biologist in Durban who completed his masters degree on microplastics that have been found in fish.

Matt
“Once you approach the smaller range of the microplastics and you head into the nanoplastics range the are so readily affected by the wind and all of that that at this point they have become environmentally ubiquitous. So microplastics at this point are everywhere.”

V/O
Macroplastics or big pieces of plastic, degrade to microplastics, which are roughly below 5mm or smaller than the size of a rice kernel, these then degrade even further into minute nanoplastics. Which are everywhere. They are not only found in the sea but they have even reached the snow in the Arctic, the pristine Pyrenees mountain peaks and the deepest trenches in the oceans.

Devi
It’s logic, if you have big plastics, they are going to become microplastics and they are going to become nanoplastics
“But 20 years ago were we even concerned about nanoplastics?”

Henk
“But now we know that plastics of all shapes and sizes are problems and probably the smaller the plastic the bigger the problem.


V/O
Henk Bouwman is a professor of Zoology at North West University. His interest in plastics was piqued when he went to the isolated Mauritian Island archipelego of St Brandon in 2010. It’s home to hundreds of thousands of seabirds.
Bouwman was researching whether pollutants were affecting the strength of the bird’s eggs shells.


Henk
“And then I saw all of this plastic lying around on the beaches there. And when we looked closer we saw that the plastics had come from the northern hemisphere, so they travelled for thousands of kilometres and that got me very concerned.”

V/O
Some of the birds were using larger pieces of plastics to create their nests. Bouman’s research findings indicated that there was a strong association with organic pollutants and the thinning of the seabirds eggshells.
The concern for scientists is that they don’t know what impact nanoplastics will have.

Henk
Plastics have a half life in the oceans of 400 years or even longer.
Plastic goes so small it actually starts acting like molecules and they can cross the membranes into the cells, they have been picked up inside cells of organisms.”

V/O
In September 2016, we analysed the impact of how microplastics were polluting our oceans and killing our marine life. KZN University was conducting research on muscles and here one could clearly see the proliferation of shiny bits of toxic microplastics when illuminated by an ultraviolet light.

Coote was a student at that time.

Matt
“A lot of the fish that are caught are primarily gutted so if you think you are removing the plastics that way, they are still in the tissue and are still being injested.”

V/O
The problem with microplastics is that they act like sponges and can concentrate toxic chemicals leached from the environment (around them).

Plastic contamination starts with the most primitive organisms. These tiny plankton are eating microplastic beads. They in turn are ingested by larger marine animals. It was just a matter of time before we realised that it was in us too.

V/O
Plastic has it’s advantages, it helps us to cook and preserve food, conduct electricity and much more. We are completely dependent on it.









Devi Link
When you are told about exposure to plastic, you think about eating plastic containers, shopping bags or children’s toys, none of us considered that there is already plastic in the water we drink, the air we breath and and the food we eat.

V/O
A recent study by Australia's University of Newcastle revealed that we consume up to a credit card or 5g of plastic a week.


V/O
We decided to see whether there was cause for concern in South Africa and we asked Coote to test how many microplastics were in the rain water in Durban.
Once we had enough volume, they were sent to Potchefstroom for testing.

Devi Link
Our rain water samples from Durban arrived here at the North West University’s microplastics laboratory a few days ago. The water is being tested for any traces of plastic particles.

V/O
The results showed that there were about 70 particles of microplastic per litre of rain water. This is because the microplastics in the air, were caught in the rain and deposited on the ground.

Devi
“Plastics in the air, what sources would they have?”

Henk
“Many sources of plastics in air, textiles as you walk across carpets, when you vacuum things, when you wash clothes, hanging up clothes, these fibres get lost from the clothing and quite a lot of these fibres then get released. When you wipe surfaces, much of that stuff is plastic or small pieces of plastic.”


Devi
“So dust particles that you see in the sunlight through the curtain is not just dust.”

Henk
“Not just dust, part of that dust is also plastics.”

Devi Link
Thousands of fibres are released with your washing from every cycle, because many washing machines lack filters which can remove microplastics from the waste water, these fibres are then carried into our water ways.



V/O
Rand Water is the largest water utility in Africa. It purifies water from it’s sources and supplies to industry, mining and municipalities. Professor Hamanth Kasan is responsible for water quality.

Devi
“Are microplastics and nanoplastics in our water, as we know it as far as Rand Water is concerned?”

Kasan
“Indeed we do have microplastics, this is not uncommon, the global literature shows and the experience indicates that microplastics have been found in almost all sources of water all over the world. However I should say that the extent that we find these microplastics in the water that we supply is very very low compared to the rest of the world.”

V/O
NWU also tests Rand Water for microplastics.

Devi
“So what are the international figures like compared to ours here?”

Kasan
“I can give you an indication of what we are finding here locally we finding compared to europe levels of some 85% lower and compared to USA some 95% lower.”

V/O
Their water is very clean with only about 0.26 pieces of microplastic per litre.
Nanoplastics are too small to test.

Devi link
But what about some of your favourite beverages, we asked the North West University to test for microplastics in a few tipples from beer, wine, soda water, sherry and bottled water.

V/O
Although the samples were tested scientifically , our aim was to test a small sample of alcohols to see if our South African beverages also contain microplastics. These are the results.

Beer up to 165 particles
Wine 93 particles
Sherry 73 particles
Soda Water 243 particles
And bottled water 13 particles per litre.

Henk
“Funny enough we found less microplastics in tap water than in bottled water.”


V/O
Prof Rialet Pieters is an ecotoxicologist at NWU.

Devi
“Are you concerned the health impact that nanoplastics could have on human health?”

Rialet
“Well Nanoplastics per se have been with humans since the dawn of plastic, I just think that we are suddenly now more aware of them, we can detect them, we can quantify them , we can identify the nature of the plastic they were made up of. I just think that they could add on to our already large exposure to a wide variety of chemicals that are foreign to the body.”

V/O
Dr Mary Gulumian of the National Institute of Occupational Health says that the bigger microplastics that are injested will just be safely excreted, but the smaller nanoplastics which we breathe in are of concern.

Devi
“Are there any studies that are able to shed some light on whether nanoplastics are able to enter the organs of animals?”

Mary
“Absolutely when we started with nano materials , it’s a matter of fact, because of science that can cross the barriers, we can inhale it even in some cases it’s been shown in animals that they can go straight to the brain from the olfactory system. Absolutely the possibility exists that they can cross from the lung to other organs.”

V/O
Despite the environmental impact, the production of plastic is increasing, some call for stricter legislation, others say education.

The World Health Organisation has said that there is no evidence so far that microplastic poses a risk to human health, but stresses more research is needed to protect future generations.












Promo 1
It’s in the food we eat, the water, we drink and the air we breath. A new study has shown that we injest 5 grams or an equivalent of a credit card of plastic every week.

Promo 2
Its been found in Arctic Snow and the deepest trenches in the ocean. It’s also in the beer, wine and water we drink. We test a few beverages to see how much microplastic we are consuming.

Promo 3
There may be more than just bubbles in your favourite tipple. Carte Blanche investigates the extent to which some beer, wine and bottled water contains minuscule plastic fragments or microplastics.

metadata.Further information: Plastic pollution is now so widespread that you may be ingesting 5g a week, the equivalent of eating a credit card, according to a study commissioned by the environmental charity WWF International. The study by Australia's University of Newcastle said the largest source of plastic ingestion was from tap and especially bottled water. In the United States, 94.4% of tap water samples contained plastic fibres, with an average of 9.6 fibres per litre. European water was less polluted, with fibres showing up in only 72.2% of water samples, and only 3.8 fibres per litre. Another major source was shellfish, which tended to be eaten whole so the plastic in their digestive system was consumed too. Nearly invisible bits of polymer were also found in beer and salt. "Since 2000, the world has produced as much plastic as all the preceding years combined, a third of which is leaked into nature," the report said. The average person could be consuming 1,769 particles of plastic every week from water alone, it said. The findings, drawn from 52 peer-reviewed studies, are the first to estimate the sheer weight of plastics consumed by individual humans: about 250g over the course of a year. The amount of plastic pollution varies by location, but nowhere is untouched, said the report. Not only are plastics polluting our oceans and waterways and killing marine life, it's in all of us. A study released last year by the Water Research Commission (WRC), done by North-West University researchers, found that our fresh water contains microplastics. The Crocodile River, which feeds the Hartbeespoort Dam before the water flows into the Limpopo, had the highest total particle, fragment and fibre counts, although the Vaal Dam water contained larger particles. The study was done on rivers in North West, Gauteng and the Free State, and included drinking and groundwater sources. Tap water in Johannesburg and Tshwane was found to contain the particles. “Generally, much lower [levels of] particles were observed in treated water compared to the raw water. Tap water samples collected from the Tshwane region seemed to have fewer fragments compared with Johannesburg,” according to the study. Following the release of the report, the department of environmental affairs said it would set up a task team of officials from the departments of trade and industry, health, and science and technology to find ways to reduce the use of these particulates. All over the world, researchers like Magadini are staring through microscopes at tiny pieces of plastic—fibers, fragments, or microbeads—that have made their way into marine and freshwater species, both wild caught and farmed. Scientists have found microplastics in 114 aquatic species, and more than half of those end up on our dinner plates. Now they are trying to determine what that means for human health. So far science lacks evidence that microplastics—pieces smaller than one-fifth of an inch—are affecting fish at the population level. Our food supply doesn’t seem to be under threat—at least as far as we know. But enough research has been done now to show that the fish and shellfish we enjoy are suffering from the omnipresence of this plastic. Every year five million to 14 million tons flow into our oceans from coastal areas. Sunlight, wind, waves, and heat break down that material into smaller bits that look—to plankton, bivalves, fish, and even whales—a lot like food. Experiments show that microplastics damage aquatic creatures, as well as turtles and birds: They block digestive tracts, diminish the urge to eat, and alter feeding behavior, all of which reduce growth and reproductive output. Their stomachs stuffed with plastic, some species starve and die. In addition to mechanical effects, microplastics have chemical impacts, because free-floating pollutants that wash off the land and into our seas—such as polychlorinated biphenyls (PCBs), polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons (PAHs), and heavy metals—tend to adhere to their surfaces.
